demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is a 22-year-old Latino man who comes to therapy carrying the memory of one split second that changed the shape of his life. Before the accident, he describes himself as confident with his hands, the kind of person who liked work that was tangible and solved problems in real time. He had started building a reputation as a capable HVAC technician, proud of showing up early, knowing his tools, and being able to step into people’s homes and leave the air working again. He felt he was on track to be dependable, someone his family could count on.

The event happens during a routine service call that should have been uneventful. He is on a ladder, working around equipment he has handled many times before, when a mistake in judgment leads to a serious injury to another person nearby. In his telling, the moment is still fragmented: the sound, the sudden movement, the realization that something irreversible has happened. He remembers the immediate rush of panic more vividly than the details of the accident itself. Afterward, he is flooded with guilt and disbelief, repeating to himself that it was not supposed to happen, that he should have seen it coming, that one error should not have been enough to change another person’s life so drastically. He says he felt his body go cold while everyone else seemed to move in slow motion around him.

In the days and weeks that follow, he cannot stay away from the scene in his mind. He replays the sequence over and over, trying to find the exact second where he could have done something different. He wakes with his jaw clenched and his chest tight, already thinking about the injury before his feet hit the floor. At work, he becomes hyperalert around ladders, wires, tools, and moving parts. He checks and rechecks his work in a way that slows him down and leaves him frustrated with himself. Even simple tasks now feel loaded with threat. He notices his hands shaking when he is expected to do something that once felt automatic. He begins to dread service calls, especially those that involve heights or tight spaces, and he finds reasons to let other technicians take the lead.

He is also haunted by the possibility that other people see him as dangerous or careless. This fear makes him pull back socially. He stops spending time as easily with friends and avoids talking about work unless he has to. At home, he sits with his phone nearby, braced for news, and when unfamiliar numbers call, his body jolts before he has even answered. He describes feeling numb much of the time, as though he is watching his life from a few steps away. When he does feel emotion, it tends to arrive all at once: shame, anger, grief, and fear in waves he has trouble naming. He is especially hard on himself, returning again and again to the thought that a “real” man should have prevented it, should have been more careful, should not have frozen.

He does not sleep well. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes in the night with his heart racing, unable to settle back down if he hears a noise outside or a truck passing by. He has trouble concentrating, especially when paperwork or instructions demand sustained attention. His appetite is inconsistent, and he often eats because he knows he should rather than from hunger. He notices that he startles easily at sudden sounds, and his body seems to be waiting for the next mistake, the next terrible consequence. At times he avoids passing by the building where the injury happened, taking longer routes even when they disrupt his day.

What stands out over time is how much of his suffering is tied to responsibility. He is not frightened only by what happened; he is trapped by the belief that he caused it and therefore deserves to live with the consequences. He wants to move forward, but moving forward feels to him like betraying the person who was hurt. He speaks carefully in session, often pausing as if he is measuring whether his words are allowed. Underneath that caution is a young man who still wants to be competent, decent, and useful, but who now carries every call, every tool, and every unexpected sound as a reminder of the moment his certainty broke.
